newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU strikes BSE aid deal despite German grumble.
newsitem.headline: EU strikes BSE aid deal despite German grumble.

text.p: European Union farm ministers overruled German opposition on Wednesday to approve a package of measures cutting beef surpluses and providing 500 million Ecus ($635 million) extra aid for farmers hit by the mad cow crisis.
France, Germany and Britain will get more than half the money, to come from savings within the bloc's farm budget.
"Important steps have been taken to curb production. Important compensatory decisions were taken," Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates told reporters after a three-day meeting.

Yates, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said the aid would supplement 850 million Ecus ($1.1 billion) agreed by EU leaders in Florence in June. Further aid was likely under long term beef reforms due in 1997, he said.

Germany, despite winning important concessions, voted against the package because it contained measures, such as incentives for traditional grass-fed herds, which it said would weaken efforts to make structural changes to cut output.

German demands to improve the terms of an EU scheme to cut beef output by marketing calves earlier and a higher premium for bulls were met. Its minister, Jochen Borchert, said he wanted the talks to take only short-term decisions to remove surpluses.

But EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said the measures, including curbs on the number of male cattle and suckler cows eligible for EU aid, would help to prepare for a long-term cut in herds and beef production.
"Without these reforms we would have even more serious difficulties," he said.

France, the EU's main beef producer, welcomed the agreement. "It's a good package...It includes young cattle and encourages extensive farming methods," French minister Philippe Vasseur told reporters.
Farmers will be able to sell beef from cattle aged between seven and nine months into EU stores in autumn 1997.
The mad cow crisis was triggered by a British government statement in March that the fatal cattle brain disease bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) might be transmitted to people.
Demand of EU beef has since fallen by 11 percent and some 400,000 tonnes of unwanted beef have been put into storage.

Britain said it was pleased with the deal. "This further substantial aid package should be very welcome to (farmers)," said Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg, noting that British farmers would get 13.1 percent of the extra aid.
